summary: The Apollo 15 Lunar Rover was a vehicle used by NASA astronauts when they went to the Moon in 1971. It was brought inside the Lunar Module. Opened up after the astronauts touched down. The rover helped astronauts David Scott and James Irwin move across the Moons surface look at places gather rock samples and carry tools for science. It made their job easier. Allowed them to go to spots that were hard to reach by walking. After finishing their mission the astronauts went back, to Earth leaving the rover on the Moon. Even though it stayed behind it became a part of the story of space exploration. The rover shows us about curiosity, bravery and the wish to find out what is unknown. It was left behind. It is never forgotten.
details:
What does it do or how does it work?
“Abandoned But Not Forgotten” is a storytelling presentation about NASA’s discarded equipment on the Moon and Mars. The story is told in first person by the Apollo 15 Lunar Rover. It follows the rover from being folded into the Lunar Module, to its first drive (when the front steering failed and the astronauts used rear-wheel steering instead), to exploring the Hadley–Apennine region with David Scott and James Irwin. It then covers being left behind when the astronauts departed, and why it still matters today. The story is organized into four themes: The Call, The Moon, Mars, and Legacy. It is available as a slide deck and as a scrolling website.

What benefits does it have?
It makes space history easier to understand and remember. Real facts, such as the 17.5 miles driven and the more than 170 pounds of samples collected, are told through a character, which works well for students and general audiences. It also shows that equipment left behind still has scientific and cultural value.

What is the intended impact?
We want people to see abandoned space hardware as a record of human achievement, not as waste. We also hope it inspires younger audiences to take an interest in space exploration and in the explorers who come next.

What tools, languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Microsoft PowerPoint for the original deck, including its built-in icon graphics (stars, rocket) and a space-themed design
  • Stock and public space photographs, with credit given where required (CC BY-ND)
  • HTML, CSS, and JavaScript for the website version, built as a single responsive page with the photos embedded
  • A laptop or desktop computer, with no special hardware needed

How is your project creative?
Instead of listing facts, it gives a machine a voice, with emotion, a problem to solve, a sad moment, and a hopeful ending. The central line, “Not everything needs to work forever to be valuable,” gives the story a message beyond the facts. The deep-space purple and gold look supports that mood, and the website adds scroll animations and a progress bar to carry the reader through the journey.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Accuracy: We kept the dates, names, distances, and mission details true to the Apollo 15 mission.
  • Audience: We used simple first-person language so students and general readers can follow it.
  • Emotional pull: We built the story arc from hope, to problem, to loss, to legacy.
  • Visuals: We chose a dark space theme and readable text, and matched photos to each part of the story.
  • Image rights: We credited sources and followed licence terms.
  • Accessibility: The web version works on phones and desktops, uses readable contrast, and describes every image in text.
